title: Controlling artificial surface heating in neutron star simulations: Application to hybrid equations of state
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures
summary: The treatment of the stellar surface in binary neutron star simulations is crucial for the accuracy of the numerical evolution and the physical reliability of the predicted observables. Numerical artifacts associated with the treatment of steep gradients near the stellar surface can produce spurious heating during the inspiral, leading to an artificial increase of the internal energy and an unphysical expansion of the neutron star. In this work, we investigate the effectiveness of the entropy-based flux-limiting (EFL) scheme in mitigating these numerical effects within the finite-difference code BAM. We perform simulations of both isolated neutron stars and binary neutron star inspirals employing a representative set of hybrid equations of state. We show that the EFL scheme significantly reduces artificial surface heating. This reduction is observed consistently across all stellar models and binary configurations considered, demonstrating that the reduction of numerical heating is a robust feature of the EFL method.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the entropy-based flux-limiting (EFL) scheme in the finite-difference code BAM to mitigate artificial surface heating in binary neutron star simulations. The EFL scheme significantly reduces spurious heating and unphysical stellar expansion across all stellar models and hybrid equations of state tested.
AI.motivation: The treatment of steep gradients at the stellar surface in binary neutron star simulations produces numerical artifacts such as spurious heating during inspiral, which artificially increases internal energy and causes unphysical expansion of the neutron star, compromising the accuracy and physical reliability of predicted observables.
AI.method: The authors implement and test the entropy-based flux-limiting (EFL) scheme within the finite-difference code BAM, and perform numerical simulations of both isolated neutron stars and binary neutron star inspirals using a representative set of hybrid equations of state.
AI.result: The EFL scheme significantly reduces artificial surface heating. This reduction is observed consistently across all stellar models and binary configurations considered, demonstrating that the reduction of numerical heating is a robust feature of the EFL method.
AI.conclusion: The EFL scheme is an effective and robust approach for mitigating numerical surface heating in binary neutron star simulations, improving the physical reliability of simulated observables.

title: A JWST/MIRI Study of Dust in a Sample of Normal Type IIP Core Collapse Supernovae
comment: Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome
summary: Core collapse supernovae (CCSNe) are invoked as major dust producers in the early Universe, yet the amount of dust they form, the timescale over which it grows, and the physical conditions that regulate the yield remain uncertain. We present a detailed JWST/MIRI mid-infrared (MIR) imaging census of 11 nearby Type IIP CCSNe spanning $\sim$1-7 yr after explosion, investigating dust emission across the different phases of their evolution. The spectral energy distributions show a coherent evolution from hot ($\sim$1500 K), 5-8 $μ$m emission at $\sim$400 d to prominent 10 and 18 $μ$m emission features at later epochs ($\sim$600-2500 d). The cool dust temperatures range from $\sim120$ to $250$ K and dust masses from $\sim10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2} M_{\odot}$. The current sample shows no statistically significant correlation between measured dust mass and peak luminosity, plateau duration, or explosion energy. SNe with early high ionization features, indicative of confined CSM, are often among the dust-rich objects in the sample. The measured 1-7 yr dust yields are insufficient to account for dust in typical $z > 6$ galaxies, but support a role for CCSNe as producers of seed dust for subsequent grain growth.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a JWST/MIRI mid-infrared imaging census of 11 nearby Type IIP core collapse supernovae observed ~1-7 years post-explosion, measuring dust emission evolution, temperatures (~120-250 K), and dust masses (~10^-4 to 10^-2 M⊙), finding that these yields are insufficient to fully explain dust in high-redshift galaxies but support CCSNe as seed dust producers.
AI.motivation: Core collapse supernovae are considered major dust producers in the early Universe, but uncertainties remain regarding the amount of dust they form, the growth timescale, and the physical conditions governing dust yield—motivating a systematic observational census of late-time SN dust emission.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI mid-infrared imaging was used to conduct a census of 11 nearby Type IIP CCSNe, constructing spectral energy distributions across multiple epochs (~1-7 yr after explosion) to characterize dust emission features, temperatures, and masses, and testing correlations with SN properties such as peak luminosity, plateau duration, explosion energy, and CSM conditions.
AI.result: The SEDs show coherent evolution from hot (~1500 K) 5-8 μm emission at ~400 d to prominent 10 and 18 μm features at later epochs. Cool dust temperatures range from ~120-250 K with dust masses of ~10^-4 to 10^-2 M⊙. No significant correlation was found between dust mass and peak luminosity, plateau duration, or explosion energy, though SNe with early high ionization features (indicating confined CSM) are often dust-rich.
AI.conclusion: The measured 1-7 yr dust yields from CCSNe are insufficient to fully account for dust in typical z > 6 galaxies, but they support a role for CCSNe as producers of seed dust that can subsequently grow in the interstellar medium.

title: Probing the $γ$-ray emission region and the connection to jet ejections in NRAO 150 with VLBI
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; accepted for publication by A&A
summary: Relativistic jets launched by active galactic nuclei are fundamental for understanding the physics of accreting supermassive black holes and their immediate environments, yet the origin of these jets remains an open question. NRAO 150 is a blazar with a complex relativistic jet morphology that evolves on short timescales due to strong projection effects, enabling detailed kinematic analysis. In this study, we utilise data by the Very Long Baseline Array and the European VLBI Network from 2010 until 2019 at 43 GHz, to understand the formation and launching processes of the jet in NRAO 150. We study the $γ$-ray and radio light-curves, together with total intensity and linear polarisation information to probe the connection between flaring events, $γ$-ray emission, and the ejection of new jet features. Furthermore, we investigate the magnetic field configuration in the innermost jet region, as captured in polarised light, to gain insights about its configuration before, during, and after a $γ$-ray flare. Our results indicate a close temporal link between the $γ$-ray flaring activity and the ejection of new VLBI jet components, suggesting that the high-energy emission is produced downstream of the VLBI core. The combined kinematic and polarimetric evidence further points to a toroidal magnetic field in the inner jet, highlighting the key role of magnetic fields in governing both jet dynamics and high-energy emission in NRAO 150.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 43 GHz VLBI observations of the blazar NRAO 150 from 2010–2019, combining kinematics, γ-ray light curves, total intensity, and linear polarisation to investigate jet formation. Results show a close temporal link between γ-ray flares and new jet component ejections, and polarimetric evidence points to a toroidal magnetic field in the inner jet, highlighting the role of magnetic fields in jet dynamics and high-energy emission.
AI.motivation: The origin of relativistic jets launched by active galactic nuclei remains an open question. NRAO 150, a blazar with a complex jet morphology evolving on short timescales due to strong projection effects, offers a unique opportunity for detailed kinematic and polarimetric analysis to understand jet formation and launching processes.
AI.method: The study utilizes VLBA and EVN observations at 43 GHz from 2010 to 2019. It combines kinematic analysis of the jet with γ-ray and radio light curves, total intensity, and linear polarisation data to probe the connection between flaring events, γ-ray emission, and jet component ejections. The magnetic field configuration in the inner jet region is investigated using polarised light before, during, and after a γ-ray flare.
AI.result: The results indicate a close temporal link between γ-ray flaring activity and the ejection of new VLBI jet components, suggesting the high-energy emission is produced downstream of the VLBI core. Kinematic and polarimetric evidence points to a toroidal magnetic field configuration in the inner jet.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the key role of magnetic fields in governing both jet dynamics and high-energy emission in NRAO 150, providing insights into the launching and formation processes of relativistic jets in AGN.

title: Resolving Nearby Supermassive Black Holes with the Black Hole Explorer
comment: accepted for publication in the Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific (PASP), 17 pages, 8 figures
summary: Recent Event Horizon Telescope results have demonstrated unique and transformative science in gravitational physics and black hole astrophysics enabled by event-horizon-scale imaging of supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Nevertheless, the angular resolution of current ground-based very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) arrays limits such studies to only two sources, precluding systematic investigations of horizon-scale emission across a nearby SMBH population. The proposed Black Hole Explorer (BHEX), a millimeter/submillimeter space VLBI mission, would overcome this limitation by delivering substantially higher angular resolution. Here, we present a series of simulated observations to assess a population of nearby horizon-scale targets accessible with BHEX. Based on a recently developed SMBH number density model, we find that BHEX could infer black hole masses for ~70-90 sources from size measurements, constrain magnetic field structures through linear polarization imaging for ~20-30 sources, and resolve black hole shadows for ~20-25 sources. Targeted observations of ~50 nearby SMBHs are expected to yield measurements for ~30 source sizes and ~10 shadows and linear-polarization patterns. These projections are supported by detailed imaging simulations of general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) models for eleven nearby SMBHs. Together, our results highlight BHEX as a powerful facility for revealing the demographics of SMBH properties across diverse accretion states, radio loudness, host galaxy environments, and viewing geometries.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates the scientific capabilities of the proposed Black Hole Explorer (BHEX), a space-based VLBI mission, for studying a population of nearby supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Based on a SMBH number density model and simulated observations, BHEX could measure BH masses for ~70-90 sources, constrain magnetic field structures for ~20-30 sources, and resolve shadows for ~20-25 sources. Detailed GRMHD imaging simulations of eleven nearby SMBHs support these projections.
AI.motivation: Current ground-based VLBI arrays limit event-horizon-scale imaging to only two sources (e.g., M87* and Sgr A*), precluding systematic demographic studies of horizon-scale emission across a nearby SMBH population. The proposed BHEX space VLBI mission would overcome this angular resolution limitation.
AI.method: The study uses a recently developed SMBH number density model to estimate the population of horizon-scale targets accessible to BHEX, combined with detailed imaging simulations of general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) models for eleven nearby SMBHs to assess feasibility of size measurements, linear polarization imaging for magnetic field constraints, and shadow resolution.
AI.result: BHEX could infer BH masses for ~70-90 sources from size measurements, constrain magnetic field structures via linear polarization for ~20-30 sources, and resolve black hole shadows for ~20-25 sources. Targeted observations of ~50 nearby SMBHs are expected to yield measurements for ~30 source sizes and ~10 shadows and linear-polarization patterns.
AI.conclusion: BHEX would be a powerful facility for revealing the demographics of SMBH properties across diverse accretion states, radio loudness, host galaxy environments, and viewing geometries, enabling systematic population studies beyond the two currently accessible sources.

title: A Critical Eddington Ratio for X-Shaped Radio Galaxies
comment: ApJ
summary: We derive a quantitative condition for the formation of X-shaped radio galaxies by evaluating the competition between black hole spin evolution and the radiative fading of relic plasma within our previously proposed framework. The simultaneous visibility of two jet axes requires that the timescale for spin evolution across zero, t_trans, be shorter than the fading timescale of relic radio emission, t_fade. We estimate the transition timescale as t_trans about 5 million /lambda yr, where lambda is the Eddington ratio, and derive a visibility timescale t_fade about equal to 5-20 Myr based on the evolution of the synchrotron break frequency for typical lobe magnetic fields and redshifts. This leads to a critical Eddington ratio lambda_crit in the range 0.3-1, above which systems can exhibit X-shaped morphologies. We show that this threshold naturally produces an environmental dependence, as radiatively efficient accretion is more readily sustained in low-density environments, while feedback in rich clusters tends to drive systems toward radiatively inefficient states with a larger fraction of systems having lambda much less than lambda_crit, suppressing XRG formation. We further demonstrate that the observed low fraction of X-shaped radio galaxies (about 1-5%) arises from the limited overlap window combined with geometric and detectability effects. These results provide a quantitative and testable extension of our previous model, linking X-shaped morphology to accretion rate and environmental conditions through a simple timescale criterion.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a quantitative timescale criterion for the formation of X-shaped radio galaxies (XRGs), showing that simultaneous visibility of two jet axes requires the spin transition timescale (t_trans ≈ 5 Myr/λ) to be shorter than the relic plasma fading timescale (t_fade ≈ 5–20 Myr), yielding a critical Eddington ratio λ_crit ≈ 0.3–1. This threshold naturally explains environmental dependence and the observed ~1–5% fraction of XRGs.
AI.motivation: To provide a quantitative, testable extension of a previously proposed framework for X-shaped radio galaxy formation by deriving the specific conditions under which the two jet axes can be simultaneously visible, and to explain the observed rarity and environmental dependence of XRGs.
AI.method: The authors compare two competing timescales: (1) the black hole spin-flip transition timescale, estimated as t_trans ≈ 5/λ Myr where λ is the Eddington ratio, and (2) the relic radio emission fading timescale, t_fade ≈ 5–20 Myr, derived from synchrotron break frequency evolution for typical lobe magnetic fields and redshifts. By setting t_trans < t_fade, they derive a critical Eddington ratio λ_crit ≈ 0.3–1 and analyze its implications for environmental dependence and observed XRG fractions including geometric and detectability effects.
AI.result: The derived critical Eddington ratio λ_crit ≈ 0.3–1 separates systems capable of exhibiting X-shaped morphologies from those that cannot. The threshold produces an environmental dependence: radiatively efficient accretion (above λ_crit) is more easily sustained in low-density environments, while feedback in rich clusters drives systems toward radiatively inefficient states, suppressing XRG formation. The observed ~1–5% fraction of XRGs is explained by the limited overlap window combined with geometric and detectability effects.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a simple timescale-based criterion linking X-shaped radio galaxy morphology to accretion rate (Eddington ratio) and environment, offering a quantitative and testable prediction that connects spin evolution, radiative fading of relic plasma, and large-scale radio morphology.

title: General relativistic hydrodynamics of stellar tidal disruptions in Kerr spacetime: methods, validation, and first applications
comment: Submitted to A&A. 12 pages, 5 figures, and 1 table (+ 8 pages, +5 figures, +1 table in Appendix)
summary: The disruption of a star by the tidal field of a super-massive black hole may provide insights into dormant and otherwise hard-to-study galactic nuclei. State-of-the-art numerical tools have not converged on the importance of the strong relativistic effects in the disruption of stars by potentially spinning black holes. We present a specialised numerical tool to perform global hydrodynamic simulations of stellar tidal disruptions in curved spacetimes. We quantify the role of impact strength and black hole spin onto the stellar structures and mass fallback rates. We adapted the code SPHINCS_BSSN to perform General Relativistic Smoothed-Particle Hydrodynamics (GRSPH) simulations of stellar tidal disruptions in Kerr metric. We coupled the code with a Newtonian self-gravity module, and we added the option to use an entropy evolution formulation to handle numerically challenging situations. Besides describing the implementation and code validation, we present a set of 18 simulations of parabolic tidal disruptions of stellar polytropes to investigate the effect of impact strength and black hole spin. We demonstrate that SPHINCS is capable of performing GRSPH simulations, reproducing benchmark tests to machine precision. Our stellar tidal disruption simulations show that the fallback rates agree with state-of-the-art modelling. Deep events result into structures where self-gravity plays no role, the mass fallback rates peak at lower values, and rise-to-peak timescales decrease with impact strength. In these cases the black hole spin affects noticeable these quantities increasing (decrease) both fallback rate peak and rise-to-peak timescale for prograde (retrograde) spin. Last, fallback rates tend to decay with the characteristic $t^{-5/3}$ on long timescales. The results show that SPHINCS can simulate high-resolution stellar tidal disruptions in Kerr metric at a reasonable computational time.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SPHINCS_BSSN, a GRSPH code adapted to perform global hydrodynamic simulations of stellar tidal disruptions by spinning (Kerr) super-massive black holes. The authors validate the code, run 18 simulations of parabolic tidal disruptions of stellar polytropes varying impact strength and black hole spin, and analyze the resulting mass fallback rates and stellar structures.
AI.motivation: Stellar tidal disruptions by super-massive black holes can reveal properties of otherwise dormant galactic nuclei, but state-of-the-art numerical tools have not converged on the importance of strong relativistic effects (e.g., black hole spin) in these events. A specialized numerical tool is needed to quantify these effects.
AI.method: The authors adapt the SPHINCS_BSSN code to perform General Relativistic Smoothed-Particle Hydrodynamics (GRSPH) simulations of stellar tidal disruptions in the Kerr metric, coupling it with a Newtonian self-gravity module and an entropy evolution formulation. They validate the implementation and run 18 simulations of parabolic tidal disruptions of stellar polytropes, varying impact strength and black hole spin.
AI.result: The code reproduces benchmark tests to machine precision. Fallback rates agree with state-of-the-art modeling. Deep events show self-gravity is negligible, lower mass fallback rate peaks, and rise-to-peak timescales that decrease with impact strength. Black hole spin noticeably affects these quantities: prograde spin increases both fallback rate peak and rise-to-peak timescale, while retrograde spin decreases them. Fallback rates decay as ~t^-5/3 on long timescales.
AI.conclusion: SPHINCS is capable of performing high-resolution GRSPH simulations of stellar tidal disruptions in Kerr metric at reasonable computational cost, providing a reliable specialized tool for studying the role of relativity and black hole spin in these events.

title: A comprehensive cluster census of Orion. An application of the Significance Mode Analysis (SigMA) algorithm
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures, 6 pages appendix. Submitted to A&A. Comments welcome
summary: Precise astrometric surveys and modern clustering algorithms are working in step to transform our view of star-forming regions. By revealing a much richer substructure than previously accessible, they pave the way for reconstructing star formation histories by accurately resolving and age-dating individual sub-populations. The Orion star-forming complex is the best-studied stellar nursery in the solar neighborhood and the nearest one currently forming massive stars. Even so, a comprehensive characterization of its substructure, including a homogeneous age mapping and extinction analysis, is still incomplete. Here, we present the most complete census of stellar populations across the Orion complex from the newest version of the SigMA algorithm and outline our additions and improvements to the algorithm that have extended its usage to distant (>300 pc) regions. We separate the Orion complex into 47 co-spatial and co-moving stellar groups comprising 11,996 reliable members, with ages ranging from 1.5 to 25 Myr. To evaluate the statistical robustness of each group, we derive cluster persistence values and individual membership probabilities for each source from 10 independent clustering repetitions. Our group memberships agree well with the literature, but SigMA consistently finds a factor of ~2-3 more members. In particular, it resolves more very young populations, such as NGC 2024, RV Orionis, B30, NGC 1977, NGC 2068, and NGC 2071, than previous algorithms. In addition to recovering 28 known clusters and three groups previously classified as substructures, we present 16 new co-eval substructure candidates of the Orion star-forming complex. This work builds up a new high-resolution time-resolved picture of Orion. This spatio-temporal map allows us to relate its stellar content to the surrounding ISM and paves the way for a detailed analysis of its star formation history in the future.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the most complete census of stellar populations in the Orion star-forming complex using an improved version of the SigMA clustering algorithm, identifying 47 co-spatial and co-moving stellar groups with 11,996 reliable members aged 1.5–25 Myr, including 16 new substructure candidates and robust membership probabilities from repeated clustering runs.
AI.motivation: Despite the Orion complex being the nearest region actively forming massive stars and the best-studied stellar nursery in the solar neighborhood, a comprehensive characterization of its substructure—including homogeneous age mapping and extinction analysis—has remained incomplete. This work aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The authors extend the SigMA algorithm to handle distant (>300 pc) regions and apply it to the Orion complex. They perform 10 independent clustering repetitions to derive persistence values and individual membership probabilities. The clustering separates the complex into 47 stellar groups and validates them against literature classifications while identifying new substructures.
AI.result: The algorithm identified 47 co-spatial and co-moving stellar groups comprising 11,996 reliable members with ages from 1.5 to 25 Myr. SigMA finds 2–3 times more members than previous algorithms, resolves more very young populations (e.g., NGC 2024, RV Orionis, B30, NGC 1977, NGC 2068, NGC 2071), recovers 28 known clusters and 3 previously classified substructures, and presents 16 new co-eval substructure candidates.
AI.conclusion: This work builds a high-resolution time-resolved (spatio-temporal) map of Orion, enabling the stellar content to be related to the surrounding ISM and laying the groundwork for a detailed future analysis of the star formation history of the region.

title: The Gamma-ray Burst Jet Energy Distribution Suggests A Quasi-universal, Weakly Magnetized Jet Evolving Over Cosmic Time
summary: We present distributions of gamma-ray burst observed and inferred properties for those GRBs with redshifts. We show that the isotropic energy distribution, which spans over four orders of magnitude, can be reproduced reasonably well under a simplistic assumption that every observed GRB originates from a quasi-universal jet with roughly the same decreasing power-law profile of energy as a function of angle, with a power-law index of $ 3 \lesssim ζ\lesssim 4$. The spread in the observed distribution can be explained by the variation in observer viewing angle alone. Furthermore, this power-law jet structure provides an even better fit to both the isotropic energy and luminosity distributions if the isotropic energy normalization evolves as a function of redshift in a manner that has been suggested by a range of previously published studies. The relatively steep power-law index of this jet is consistent with the structure predicted by simulations of weakly magnetized jets in collapsars, whereas simulations of hydrodynamic jets predict a structure shallower than what we find here. The predicted afterglow light curves within this model framework show steepening behavior at times commensurate with observed jet break times.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes observed and inferred properties of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) with known redshifts, showing that the isotropic energy distribution across four orders of magnitude can be well explained by a quasi-universal jet model with a steep power-law energy profile (index 3-4) as a function of angle, with spread arising solely from variations in observer viewing angle. The fit improves when accounting for redshift evolution of the isotropic energy normalization, and the steep structure matches predictions from weakly magnetized jet simulations in collapsars.
AI.motivation: To understand the intrinsic jet structure of gamma-ray bursts by testing whether a simple quasi-universal power-law jet model can explain the observed diversity in GRB isotropic energy and luminosity distributions, and to constrain the angular energy profile of GRB jets.
AI.method: The authors compare observed isotropic energy and luminosity distributions of GRBs with redshifts against predictions from a quasi-universal jet model with a decreasing power-law energy profile as a function of angle (constrained to power-law index ζ between 3 and 4). They test the model both with a fixed isotropic energy normalization and with a redshift-evolving normalization, and compare the inferred jet structure with predictions from different types of collapsar jet simulations.
AI.result: A quasi-universal jet with a steep power-law index of 3 to 4 reproduces the observed isotropic energy distribution well, with the spread explained purely by viewing angle variation. The fit improves further when redshift evolution of the isotropic energy normalization is included. The steep index is consistent with weakly magnetized jet simulations but conflicts with hydrodynamic jet predictions. Predicted afterglow light curves show steepening at times consistent with observed jet break times.
AI.conclusion: GRB jet structure is consistent with a quasi-universal power-law profile with a steep index (ζ≈3-4), favoring weakly magnetized jets in collapsars over purely hydrodynamic jets. The model naturally explains the observed energy/luminosity spreads and afterglow jet break behavior without requiring a diverse range of intrinsic jet opening angles.

title: Interacting stellar winds feeding Sgr A*: from the system of mass-losing stars to the binary IRS 16SW
comment: Proceedings for the IAU Symposium 405: "Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time". 5 pages and 2 figures
summary: The discovery of cold structures around Sgr A* has challenged our understanding of the gas dynamics and thermodynamic state of the plasma in its vicinity. This work aims to constrain the conditions for the formation of such structures, namely the cold disc-like structure and the recently discovered G-1-2-3 complex. We conduct hydrodynamic simulations of the observed Wolf-Rayet stars feeding Sgr A*. Our simulations show that the plasma chemical composition is crucial for determining the medium properties. We demonstrate that the formation of a cold disc is possible for chemical compositions that are consistent with observational constraints. However, it is not possible to reproduce all the properties of the observed disc which might suggest the interaction with another structure. Additionally, we present our first results on the hydrodynamic modelling of IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary. This is the first step to develop a realistic model on the formation of the G-1-2-3 complex.

AI.tldr: This paper uses hydrodynamic simulations of Wolf-Rayet stars feeding Sgr A* to constrain conditions for forming cold structures around the Galactic center (a cold disc and the G-1-2-3 complex). The study finds that plasma chemical composition is critical for medium properties, and that a cold disc can form under observationally consistent compositions, though reproducing all observed disc properties may require interaction with another structure. It also presents first results modeling IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary, as a stepping stone toward a realistic model of the G-1-2-3 complex.
AI.motivation: The discovery of cold structures around Sgr A* challenges current understanding of gas dynamics and the thermodynamic state of the plasma near the supermassive black hole. The authors aim to constrain the physical conditions required for forming such cold structures, including the cold disc-like structure and the G-1-2-3 complex.
AI.method: Hydrodynamic simulations of Wolf-Rayet stars feeding Sgr A* are conducted to model the plasma environment. The simulations explore the role of plasma chemical composition in determining medium properties. The modeling also includes first hydrodynamic treatment of IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary system.
AI.result: The simulations demonstrate that the plasma chemical composition is crucial for determining medium properties. The formation of a cold disc is possible for chemical compositions consistent with observational constraints, but the full observed disc properties cannot be reproduced, suggesting possible interaction with another structure. Initial results from modeling IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary are presented.
AI.conclusion: Cold disc formation around Sgr A* is feasible under observationally consistent chemical compositions, though discrepancies with observations hint at additional physical processes or interactions. The hydrodynamic modeling of IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary represents the first step toward a realistic formation model for the G-1-2-3 complex.

title: Broadband emission of microquasar remnants
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics. 12 pages + appendices
summary: Microquasar remnants (MQRs), the long-lived cocoons inflated by extinct microquasar jets, have recently been proposed as hidden Galactic PeVatrons capable of producing ultra-high-energy gamma rays without an active central engine. While hadronic interactions can account for bright gamma-ray emission from nearby clouds, the direct detection of MQRs remains challenging because their intrinsic emission is expected to be extended and of low surface brightness. In this work, we explore the broadband emission of MQRs by focusing on the leptonic component confined within the cocoon and on particle interactions in the shocked shell surrounding it. We model the injection and time-dependent transport of relativistic particles, including stochastic re-acceleration driven by internal turbulence, treated as a second-order Fermi process. We consider sub-Eddington and super-Eddington microquasar systems and compute the resulting non-thermal emission from radio to gamma-ray energies, together with the thermal soft X-ray emission produced in the shocked shell. In the super-Eddington case, the intrinsic emission reaches peak values of $νL_ν\sim 10^{35}-10^{36}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$, whereas sub-Eddington remnants are typically several orders of magnitude fainter. At 1.3 GHz, the modeled cocoon surface brightness is of order $Σ_ν\sim 10^{-19}\,{\rm W\,m^{-2}\,Hz^{-1}\,sr^{-1}}$ for young powerful remnants and decreases rapidly as the remnant evolves. We find that the direct detectability of MQRs is therefore controlled mainly by surface brightness rather than by integrated luminosity. Powerful remnants may be detectable as extended synchrotron radio cocoons and shell-dominated soft X-ray structures, whereas sub-Eddington remnants are expected to be much harder to identify directly. Our results suggest that MQRs may constitute a hidden population of extended Galactic non-thermal sources.

AI.tldr: This paper models the broadband (radio to gamma-ray) non-thermal emission of microquasar remnants (MQRs)—long-lived cocoons inflated by extinct microquasar jets—including leptonic particle transport, stochastic re-acceleration via second-order Fermi processes, and thermal soft X-ray emission from the shocked shell. It finds intrinsic peak luminosities of ~10^35–10^36 erg/s for super-Eddington systems (orders of magnitude brighter than sub-Eddington ones) and shows that direct detectability is governed by surface brightness (~10^-19 W m^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1 at 1.3 GHz for young powerful remnants) rather than integrated luminosity. Powerful MQRs may be directly detectable as extended radio cocoons and shell-dominated X-ray structures, while sub-Eddington remnants remain difficult to observe, suggesting MQRs form a hidden population of extended Galactic non-thermal sources.
AI.motivation: Microquasar remnants have been proposed as hidden Galactic PeVatrons capable of producing ultra-high-energy gamma rays without an active central engine, yet direct detection is challenging because their intrinsic emission is extended and of low surface brightness. This work aims to quantitatively explore the broadband emission and detectability of MQRs by modeling both leptonic and hadronic particle processes within the cocoon and shocked shell.
AI.method: The authors model injection and time-dependent transport of relativistic particles within MQR cocoons, including stochastic re-acceleration from internal turbulence treated as a second-order Fermi process. They consider both sub-Eddington and super-Eddington microquasar systems and compute non-thermal emission across radio to gamma-ray energies, along with thermal soft X-ray emission from the shocked shell surrounding the cocoon.
AI.result: Super-Eddington remnants reach peak intrinsic luminosities of νL_ν ~ 10^35–10^36 erg/s, while sub-Eddington remnants are orders of magnitude fainter. At 1.3 GHz, modeled cocoon surface brightness is on the order of 10^-19 W m^-2 Hz^-1 sr^-1 for young powerful remnants and declines rapidly with evolution. Direct detectability is controlled primarily by surface brightness rather than integrated luminosity; powerful remnants may be seen as extended synchrotron radio cocoons and shell-dominated soft X-ray structures, whereas sub-Eddington remnants are much harder to identify.
AI.conclusion: MQRs may constitute a hidden population of extended Galactic non-thermal sources, with powerful remnants being potentially directly detectable through extended radio and soft X-ray emission, and their detectability determined mainly by surface brightness constraints.

title: Diverse ionized gas conditions in a dynamically hot, interacting galaxy at $z = 9.31$ revealed by JWST/NIRSpec IFU
comment: Submitted to MNRAS, 12 pages
summary: We present a spatially and spectrally resolved study of an interacting galaxy, Gz9p3 at $z=9.31$, using the James Webb Space Telescope NIRSpec/G395H IFU observation with high-spectral resolution ($R\approx 2700$) mode. Gz9p3 consists of two sub-regions (`core' and `tail'), which show stark contrast in their physical properties. The HII regions in the core are characterized by high electron density ($n_{e}\gtrsim2900$ cm$^{-3}$), low gas-phase metallicity ($0.25$ dex below the mass-metallicity relation), and yet relatively low specific star formation rate (sSFR) among the system. On the other hand, the tail exhibits low electron density ($n_{e}<70$ cm$^{-3}$), relatively high gas-phase metallicity that is consistent with the mass-metallicity relation, and high sSFR. The integrated spectrum thus shows the properties inbetween these two regions. No evidence of ordered rotation in ionized gas is found, suggesting that Gz9p3 is a dynamically hot system. Finally, we find ionized gas outflows characterized by the secondary [OIII]5007 line component throughout most of the system. The outflow velocity is below the escape velocity, making Gz9p3 one of the first galactic systems experiencing a galactic fountain. Overall, our findings indicate that this system is in a phase in which the pristine gas is falling efficiently into the core, diluting the gas metallicity, and enhancing star formation and outflows after the galaxy interaction.

AI.tldr: A spatially and spectrally resolved JWST NIRSpec/G395H IFU study of the interacting galaxy Gz9p3 at z=9.31 reveals stark physical contrasts between its core (high electron density, low metallicity, low sSFR) and tail (low density, high metallicity, high sSFR). The system shows no ordered rotation, exhibits ionized gas outflows below escape velocity (a galactic fountain), and is interpreted as a post-merger phase with pristine gas infalling into the core, diluting metallicity and enhancing star formation.
AI.motivation: To understand galaxy formation and evolution in the early universe by studying the spatially resolved physical properties of an interacting galaxy at z=9.31, a redshift where such detailed analysis is only now possible with JWST.
AI.method: JWST NIRSpec/G395H IFU observations with high spectral resolution (R≈2700), used to perform spatially and spectrally resolved analysis of electron density, gas-phase metallicity, specific star formation rate, kinematics, and outflows across the two sub-regions (core and tail) of Gz9p3.
AI.result: The core has high electron density (ne≳2900 cm⁻³), metallicity 0.25 dex below the mass-metallicity relation, and low sSFR; the tail has low density (ne<70 cm⁻³), near-relation metallicity, and high sSFR. No ordered rotation is found (dynamically hot system). Ionized gas outflows from a secondary [OIII]5007 component exist throughout, with velocities below the escape velocity—a galactic fountain.
AI.conclusion: Gz9p3 is in a post-interaction phase where pristine gas is efficiently accreted into the core, diluting its metallicity while enhancing star formation and driving sub-escape-velocity outflows (galactic fountain), providing insight into early galaxy assembly via mergers.

title: Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals in Gaseous Disks
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, supplementary mathematica notebook in the source file. Comments welcome!
summary: Gravitational waves from extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are precise probes of the environment of the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) they orbit. If an SMBH is actively accreting, the surrounding gaseous disk can impart hydrodynamic torques on and assist the formation of EMRIs within it. Such disk-EMRI interactions could leave measurable imprints on future observations by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), and potentially provide a route to constrain disk properties using gravitational wave observations. We present herein a detailed relativistic analysis of these hydrodynamic interactions using linear theory. We first derive a Lagrangian governing the evolution of spiral density waves in the disk and use it to formulate a balance law for the transfer of angular momentum between the EMRI and disk. We then develop a stable numerical scheme which can be used to treat corotation resonances and find modal solutions in thin disks up to very large azimuthal numbers. Using this numerical scheme, we explore how SMBH spins, EMRI semi-major axes, disk scale heights, sound speed gradients, and surface density gradients affect the interaction between accretion disks and circular EMRIs. Our results show that relativistic effects substantially alter disk-EMRI interactions once the secondary orbit is within $\mathcal{O}(25)$ Schwarzschild radii from the SMBH. Comparing our numerical results with recent analytical models suggests that the impact of pressure gradients and softening of the gravitational potential is important for disks with finite thickness and cannot be captured by tuning the torque cutoff parameters in the analytical models. The framework provided here will help analyze the formation scenarios of EMRIs and build relativistically accurate waveform models of disk-EMRI interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a detailed relativistic linear-theory analysis of hydrodynamic interactions between accretion disks and extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), developing a Lagrangian framework and stable numerical scheme to study how disk properties and relativistic effects influence disk-EMRI angular momentum transfer. Results show relativistic effects become significant within ~25 Schwarzschild radii, and that pressure gradients and gravitational potential softening in finite-thickness disks cannot be captured by simple analytical torque cutoff tuning.
AI.motivation: EMRIs in actively accreting supermassive black holes interact with surrounding gaseous disks via hydrodynamic torques, which could leave measurable imprints on future LISA observations. A detailed understanding of these disk-EMRI interactions is needed to constrain disk properties through gravitational wave observations and to build accurate formation scenario models.
AI.method: The authors derive a Lagrangian for spiral density wave evolution in the disk using linear theory, formulate an angular momentum balance law between the EMRI and disk, and develop a stable numerical scheme to treat corotation resonances and find modal solutions in thin disks at large azimuthal numbers. They systematically explore the effects of SMBH spins, EMRI semi-major axes, disk scale heights, sound speed gradients, and surface density gradients on circular EMRIs.
AI.result: Relativistic effects substantially alter disk-EMRI interactions when the secondary orbit is within approximately 25 Schwarzschild radii from the SMBH. Comparisons with analytical models reveal that pressure gradients and gravitational potential softening in finite-thickness disks are important and cannot be captured by tuning torque cutoff parameters in analytical models.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a relativistically accurate foundation for analyzing EMRI formation scenarios and building waveform models of disk-EMRI interactions suitable for future LISA observations.

title: The VariableTNG project: Unveiling the physical drivers of galaxy quenching
comment: Total: 18 pages, 12 main text + 5 appendixs. 14 figures, 8 main text + 6 appendix
summary: Understanding the physical processes that regulate galaxy quenching is a key challenge in galaxy formation and evolution. The VariableTNG (VTNG) project provides a laboratory to investigate these processes, as it systematically varies eight parameters of galaxy formation while keeping the initial conditions fixed, allowing the effects of individual feedback prescriptions to be isolated. We use interpretable machine-learning techniques as a tool to identify the parameters that most strongly regulate the quenched galaxy fraction. Our goal is to quantify the relative importance of the galaxy formation and feedback parameters that regulate the quenched galaxy fraction at z=0, determine how their influence changes across stellar mass and environment. We compute the quenched galaxy fraction for 26 VTNG boxes as a function of stellar mass, black hole mass, and gas mass, considering both the total galaxy population and separate samples of central and satellite galaxies. We train Random Forest regressors to predict the variation of the quenched fraction relative to the TNG100-1 model and use SHAP values to quantify both the magnitude and direction of the influence of each parameter. Our analysis reveals that only a small subset of the VTNG parameters dominates the variance of the quenched fraction. The stellar feedback wind parameter is the primary driver at low stellar masses, while its importance gradually shifts toward AGN-related parameters at higher masses. The supernova temperature also plays an important role at both extremes of the stellar-mass range. This transition persists when the galaxy population is divided into central and satellite systems. Comparisons with observational measurements further suggest that variations in these feedback parameters may contribute to the discrepancies between the fiducial TNG100-1 model and the observed passive galaxy population.

AI.tldr: The VariableTNG project systematically varies eight galaxy formation parameters to study galaxy quenching. Using Random Forest regressors and SHAP values on the quenched galaxy fraction across 26 simulations, the authors find that only a small subset of parameters dominates quenching variance: stellar feedback wind parameters drive quenching at low stellar masses, AGN-related parameters dominate at high masses, and supernova temperature is important at both extremes. This parameter transition persists for central and satellite galaxies separately, and these variations may explain discrepancies between the fiducial TNG100-1 model and observed passive galaxies.
AI.motivation: Understanding the physical processes that regulate galaxy quenching is a key challenge in galaxy formation and evolution. The authors aim to identify which galaxy formation and feedback parameters most strongly regulate the quenched galaxy fraction and to quantify how their influence changes across stellar mass and environment.
AI.method: The authors use the VariableTNG (VTNG) project, which varies eight galaxy formation parameters with fixed initial conditions to isolate individual feedback effects. They compute the quenched galaxy fraction for 26 VTNG boxes as a function of stellar mass, black hole mass, and gas mass, for total, central, and satellite galaxy populations. They train Random Forest regressors to predict quenched fraction variations relative to the TNG100-1 fiducial model and employ SHAP values to quantify both magnitude and direction of each parameter's influence.
AI.result: Only a small subset of VTNG parameters dominates the variance of the quenched fraction. The stellar feedback wind parameter is the primary driver at low stellar masses, while importance shifts toward AGN-related parameters at higher masses. Supernova temperature is important at both extremes of the stellar-mass range. This transition persists when dividing populations into central and satellite galaxies. Comparisons with observations suggest these feedback parameter variations may contribute to discrepancies between TNG100-1 and observed passive galaxy populations.
AI.conclusion: The analysis identifies a clear stellar-mass-dependent transition in which feedback parameters dominate galaxy quenching, from stellar wind feedback at low masses to AGN feedback at high masses, with supernova temperature relevant at both extremes. These findings suggest that tuning a small subset of feedback parameters could reconcile simulations with observations of passive galaxies.

title: The X-Ray Continuum Emission Region in the Lensed Quasar SDSS J133907.23+131038.6 is Much Smaller than the Accretion Disk
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We analyze microlensing variability in 15 seasons of optical monitoring data and 4 epochs of new X-ray observations of the doubly-imaged gravitationally lensed quasar SDSS J133907.23+131038.6 to place empirical constraints on the size and structure of that system's X-ray and optical continuum emission regions. Employing a Bayesian Monte Carlo method, we analyzed ground-based optical light curves to constrain the half-light radius of the far-UV source $\log(r_{\rm 1/2, FUV}/{\rm cm})=15.78^{+0.26}_{-0.28}$ at 193 nm, the rest-frame center of the {\it r}-band, assuming a $60^\circ$ inclination angle. This size corresponds to $\sim100\,{\it r}_{\rm g}$ for a $4.0 \times 10^{8} \: {\rm M_{\odot}}$ black hole. We measured the half-light radius of the full band ($0.2-8.0 \: {\rm keV}$) X-ray continuum emission region $\log(r_{\rm 1/2, X_{full}}/{\rm cm})=14.32^{+0.23}_{-0.31}$, a size measurement that is consistent with the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) in the Schwarzschild metric.Two shifted Fe K$α$ lines caused by microlensing are detected in the stacked spectrum of image A at 5.9 and 8.9~keV at $>99\%$ significance.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 15 seasons of optical monitoring and 4 epochs of X-ray observations of the gravitationally lensed quasar SDSS J1339+1310 to constrain the sizes of its X-ray and optical continuum emission regions via microlensing. The optical far-UV emission region has a half-light radius of log(r/cm)=15.78 at 193 nm (~100 rg for a 4x10^8 Msun black hole), while the X-ray emitting region in the 0.2-8.0 keV band has a half-light radius of log(r/cm)=14.32, consistent with the ISCO in the Schwarzschild metric. Two microlensed Fe K-alpha lines are detected at 5.9 and 8.9 keV at >99% significance.
AI.motivation: To place empirical constraints on the size and structure of the X-ray and optical continuum emission regions in a gravitationally lensed quasar, providing insight into the accretion disk geometry and emission mechanisms around supermassive black holes.
AI.method: Bayesian Monte Carlo microlensing analysis of 15 seasons of ground-based optical light curves combined with 4 epochs of new X-ray observations of the doubly-imaged lensed quasar SDSS J133907.23+131038.6.
AI.result: The far-UV source half-light radius is log(r/cm)=15.78 (at 193 nm, ~100 rg for a 4x10^8 Msun black hole). The full X-ray band (0.2-8.0 keV) half-light radius is log(r/cm)=14.32, consistent with the Schwarzschild ISCO. Two microlensed, shifted Fe K-alpha lines are detected at 5.9 and 8.9 keV at >99% significance.
AI.conclusion: The X-ray continuum emission originates from a region extremely close to the black hole (consistent with the ISCO), while the optical/UV emission originates from a much larger region (~100 gravitational radii), consistent with standard accretion disk models. The detection of microlensed Fe K-alpha lines provides additional evidence for small-scale X-ray reprocessing regions in the inner accretion flow.

title: Measuring Simulated Circumgalactic Medium Turbulence with Emission-Weighted Projected Velocity Structure Functions in FOGGIE
comment: 25 pages, 17 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: The spatially-resolved kinematics of line emission from the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of a galaxy can contain information about the CGM turbulence, which may play an important role in galaxy evolution. Due to the region's diffuse nature, there have been limited observations of low-redshift CGM emission until recent efforts that use spatially-resolved emission line kinematics to probe CGM turbulence. We use velocity structure functions (VSFs) as a measure for the properties of turbulence using the high-resolution cosmological zoom-in FOGGIE simulations. We focus on the location of the "turnover" in the VSF slope, often used as a measurement of the turbulence driving scale, and study how resolution, measurement area size, projection effects, and gas temperature influence the inferred CGM turbulence driving scale. We find that projection significantly lowers the VSF normalization but we do not find significant differences in the slope between 3D VSFs and emission-weighted projected 2D VSFs. We find that the size of the area used to measure the VSF, which can be thought of as the size of the emission nebula for a given instrument sensitivity, correlates directly with the turnover location in the VSF. These dependencies should be considered when using VSFs to interpret CGM turbulence from emission data, as projection, resolution and sensitivity constraints, and the temperature of the gas probed will all have a measurable effect on the VSF structure and the corresponding inferred turbulent properties.

AI.tldr: This paper uses FOGGIE cosmological zoom-in simulations to study how velocity structure functions (VSFs) can be used to probe turbulence in the circumgalactic medium (CGM). The authors investigate how resolution, measurement area size, projection effects, and gas temperature affect the inferred turbulence driving scale from VSFs, finding that projection lowers VSF normalization, measurement area size correlates with turnover location, and all these factors measurably impact VSF interpretation.
AI.motivation: The CGM is diffuse and difficult to observe, with limited low-redshift emission observations. Understanding CGM turbulence is important because it may play a significant role in galaxy evolution. The authors aim to validate and characterize the use of VSFs as a diagnostic tool for measuring CGM turbulence driving scales from emission line data.
AI.method: The authors use high-resolution cosmological zoom-in FOGGIE simulations to compute velocity structure functions (VSFs) of CGM line emission. They systematically compare 3D VSFs with emission-weighted projected 2D VSFs, examining the turnover location in the VSF slope (interpreted as the turbulence driving scale) across varying resolution, measurement area sizes, projection geometries, and gas temperatures.
AI.result: Projection significantly lowers VSF normalization but does not substantially change the slope between 3D and emission-weighted projected 2D VSFs. The measurement area size—analogous to the emission nebula size for a given sensitivity—correlates directly with the VSF turnover location. Projection, resolution, sensitivity constraints, and gas temperature all measurably affect VSF structure and inferred turbulence properties.
AI.conclusion: When using VSFs to interpret CGM turbulence from emission-line observations, one must account for projection effects, resolution and sensitivity limitations, measurement area size, and the temperature of the probed gas, as each influences the measured VSF and the resulting inferred turbulent driving scale.

title: Surface gravity wave on a neutron star ocean trapped around a magnetic pole
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures
summary:
A warm neutron star is expected to have a fluid "ocean" of heavy elements at its outermost part of the outer crust. As is on the terrestrial ocean, the neutron star ocean also has surface gravity waves. Around a magnetic pole of a star, the ocean may have a dip due to the strong magnetic pressure coming into play in the hydrostatic balance of the ocean. The dip enables the surface gravity wave to be trapped around the magnetic pole to form eigenmodes. The frequency of the mode is much lower than the dynamical frequency at the stellar surface, owing to the weak Coriolis force and the gradient in the ocean's depth that makes the eigenmodes present. We solve the equation of surface gravity waves in the local $β$-plane approximation and obtain the spectrum of discrete eigenmodes. We see that there are no axisymmetric modes and that the mode frequency decreases and asymptotes to zero as the number of nodes of the corresponding eigenfunction increases. This is reminiscent of the g-modes in the context of asteroseismology.
  Observations of X-ray binaries containing neutron stars reveal that some of the systems exhibit low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) whose frequency is $1-10^3$mHz. We investigate whether the eigenmodes considered here may explain the low-frequency QPO spectrum. It is suggested that some of the QPOs in the system whose neutron star spins at the period less than $10$s may be consistent with the model. As far as the spin period is larger than $10$s, the eigenmode frequencies are too low to explain the observed QPOs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates surface gravity wave eigenmodes trapped around magnetic poles in the ocean of a warm neutron star, showing they emerge due to magnetic pressure-induced depth dips. The mode frequencies are low, decrease with node number, and asymptote to zero. Comparing with observed low-frequency QPOs in X-ray binaries, the model can explain QPOs only for systems with spin periods less than 10 seconds.
AI.motivation: To provide a physical model for the origin of low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (1-10^3 mHz) observed in some neutron star X-ray binaries, by exploring trapped surface gravity wave eigenmodes in the neutron star ocean near magnetic poles.
AI.method: The authors solve the surface gravity wave equation within the local β-plane approximation, accounting for the depth gradient and weak Coriolis force in the ocean's hydrostatic balance near the magnetic pole, to derive the discrete eigenmode spectrum.
AI.result: The spectrum contains no axisymmetric modes; eigenmode frequencies decrease and asymptote to zero as the number of eigenfunction nodes increases. The model can explain certain low-frequency QPOs in systems with neutron star spin periods less than 10 seconds, but fails for longer spin periods where predicted frequencies are too low.
AI.conclusion: Trapped surface gravity waves around magnetic poles may account for some low-frequency QPOs in fast-spinning neutron star systems (spin period < 10 s), while the mechanism is insufficient for slower rotators.

title: The VariableTNG project: how baryonic mechanisms shape galaxy properties
summary: We use 50 Sobol-sampled VariableTNG simulations, varying eight subgrid parameters at fixed cosmology and initial conditions, to determine which baryonic processes regulate galaxies and black holes at $z=6$ and $z=8$. We compare the simulations with recent high-redshift measurements of the stellar mass function, star-forming main sequence, stellar and gas-phase mass-metallicity relations, stellar mass-size relation, and black-hole host and accretion properties. The simulations reproduce several broad trends in these observables, although differences remain in gas-phase metallicity, galaxy size, and the most extreme black-hole populations. Given the substantial uncertainties in both the physical modelling and the observational inference of high-redshift galaxy properties, we regard these differences as diagnostic tensions rather than definitive model failures. Random-forest analyses reveal a clear hierarchy in parameter sensitivity. The abundance of low-mass galaxies is regulated primarily by stellar feedback, particularly the supernova temperature $T_{\mathrm{SN}}$ and thermal wind fraction $τ_{\mathrm{w}}$, whereas the sensitivity of the scatter in the star-forming main sequence is weaker and redshift dependent. The high-accretion tail of black-hole growth depends on black-hole seeding and feedback parameters, but also on $T_{\mathrm{SN}}$, suggesting that stellar feedback indirectly regulates rapid black-hole growth through its impact on the available gas supply. Although cosmic variance can obscure these intrinsic responses in independent small volumes, our controlled experiment identifies stellar feedback as a common physical link between early low-mass galaxy formation and rapid black-hole growth.

AI.tldr: This paper uses 50 Sobol-sampled VariableTNG simulations with varying subgrid parameters to identify which baryonic processes regulate galaxies and black holes at z=6 and z=8, finding that stellar feedback (particularly supernova temperature and thermal wind fraction) is the dominant regulator of both low-mass galaxy abundance and rapid black-hole growth.
AI.motivation: To determine which baryonic processes are responsible for regulating galaxy and black hole properties at high redshift (z=6 and z=8), where observational constraints are uncertain and subgrid physics is poorly understood.
AI.method: Running 50 Sobol-sampled VariableTNG simulations with eight varying subgrid parameters at fixed cosmology and initial conditions, then comparing outputs to high-redshift observations (stellar mass function, star-forming main sequence, mass-metallicity relations, mass-size relation, black-hole properties) and applying random-forest analyses to establish parameter sensitivity hierarchies.
AI.result: The simulations reproduce several observed trends with residual tensions in gas-phase metallicity, galaxy size, and extreme black-hole populations. Random-forest analysis shows low-mass galaxy abundance is primarily governed by stellar feedback (supernova temperature and thermal wind fraction), while black-hole high-accretion growth depends on seeding, feedback parameters, and also supernova temperature—revealing stellar feedback as an indirect regulator of rapid black-hole growth via gas supply.
AI.conclusion: Stellar feedback serves as a common physical link between early low-mass galaxy formation and rapid black-hole growth at high redshift, though cosmic variance and observational uncertainties mean remaining discrepancies are diagnostic tensions rather than model failures.

title: AT 2020afjz (TSS2020a): The First Fast Extragalactic Transient Discovered by TESS
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to AAS journals
summary: We report the discovery of AT 2020afjz (TSS2020a): the first hour-scale extragalactic transient discovered in optical wavelengths whose complete evolution -- from explosion onset to decay -- is temporally resolved, and the first such transient discovered by TESS. AT 2020afjz was identified as a $>10σ$ detection in the pilot HiLaTS program run within the TESSELLATE Sky Survey, which blindly searches for transient phenomena in TESS data with the TESSELLATE pipeline. Through cross-matching with legacy imaging, we associate it with DES J042144.37$-$383311.3, a member of an interacting galaxy pair at $z_{\rm phot}=0.67^{+0.07}_{-0.10}$. While AT 2020afjz is similar in duration and brightness to GRB afterglows, it exhibits a slow rise time of $\sim1$ hr and lasts for only 2.4 hr above the half-max brightness; modeling the TESS light curve with VegasAfterglow finds that it is best described as either an on-axis "dirty-fireball" or off-axis orphan afterglow. Each of these rare classifications hinge upon a non-detection at gamma-ray energies, but as Fermi-GBM was Earth-occulted at the time of explosion, AT 2020afjz's gamma-quiet nature cannot be definitively confirmed. Regardless, AT 2020afjz demonstrates TESS's power to discover fast extragalactic transients, and heralds a new population awaiting discovery with TESSELLATE.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of AT 2020afjz, the first hour-scale extragalactic optical transient with fully resolved temporal evolution, discovered by TESS via the HiLaTS pilot program within the TESSELLATE Sky Survey. It is likely an on-axis "dirty fireball" or off-axis orphan gamma-ray burst afterglow, but its gamma-ray classification cannot be confirmed because Fermi-GBM was Earth-occulted during the explosion.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that TESS can discover fast extragalactic transients on hour timescales, opening a new observational window for phenomena that are too rapid and optically faint for traditional surveys.
AI.method: The transient was discovered via a blind search of TESS data using the TESSELLATE pipeline within the HiLaTS pilot program, identified at >10σ significance. It was cross-matched with legacy imaging to identify its host galaxy, and the TESS light curve was modeled with the VegasAfterglow code to classify the explosion type (on-axis dirty fireball vs. off-axis orphan afterglow).
AI.result: AT 2020afjz is associated with DES J042144.37−383311.3, a member of an interacting galaxy pair at z_phot ≈ 0.67. It has a slow rise of ~1 hour and a duration of 2.4 hours above half-maximum brightness. The light curve is best fit by either an on-axis "dirty fireball" or an off-axis orphan afterglow model, but a definitive gamma-ray classification is impossible because Fermi-GBM was Earth-occulted at explosion time.
AI.conclusion: AT 2020afjz demonstrates TESS's capability to discover fast extragalactic transients with fully resolved light curves and heralds a new population of hour-scale events awaiting discovery with the TESSELLATE survey.

title: Diffuse Dwarf Galaxies in Galaxy Clusters: I. Stellar Populations and Radial Gradients
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We use Keck/KCWI spectroscopy to study one ultra-diffuse galaxy (UDG) and five Nearly-UDGs (NUDGEs) in the Perseus cluster, together with an additional UDG in the Coma cluster. As the first paper in a series, we focus on the global and radial stellar population properties of our sample. We find that these galaxies host intermediate-to old stellar populations, with typical ages of ~7 Gyr, low metallicities ([M/H]$\simeq$ -0.9 dex), and enhanced [Mg/Fe] abundances (~0.3 dex), consistent with previous studies. Six galaxies lie within the scatter of the present-day mass-metallicity relation (MZR), whereas the Coma UDG (DF11) is more consistent with the MZR of high-z galaxies (z ~ 2). We find no strong correlation between global stellar population properties and cluster infall parameters, suggesting that any environmental impact is not easily traceable through integrated stellar populations. We go one step further and measure radial gradients for three galaxies. Two show flat age and mildly negative metallicity gradients, similar to classical dwarfs, while one shows a rising metallicity profile as recently found in other UDGs. Comparing with classical dwarfs, we find a continuous correlation between metallicity gradient and globular cluster (GC) richness, where more GC-rich systems tend to show rising profiles. We propose that preferential tidal disruption of GCs in the inner regions of galaxies naturally produces rising metallicity profiles, unlike GC-poor classical dwarfs. This mechanism, potentially coupled with strong stellar feedback from early concentrated star formation, may explain the unusual rising metallicity profiles observed in GC-rich UDGs/NUDGEs.

AI.tldr: This study uses Keck/KCWI spectroscopy to analyze the stellar populations of six ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) and Nearly-UDGs (NUDGEs) in the Perseus and Coma clusters, finding intermediate-to-old ages (~7 Gyr), low metallicities (~-0.9 dex), and enhanced [Mg/Fe] (~0.3 dex). The authors measure radial gradients for three galaxies and find a continuous correlation between metallicity gradient and globular cluster richness, proposing that preferential tidal disruption of inner GCs explains rising metallicity profiles in GC-rich UDGs.
AI.motivation: To understand the stellar population properties and formation mechanisms of ultra-diffuse galaxies in dense cluster environments, particularly investigating their ages, metallicities, and metallicity gradients to constrain their evolutionary history.
AI.method: Keck/KCWI spectroscopy of six UDGs/NUDGEs in the Perseus cluster and one UDG in the Coma cluster. Global stellar population properties (age, [M/H], [Mg/Fe]) are derived, compared to mass-metallicity relations, correlated with cluster infall parameters, and radial gradients are measured for three galaxies and compared against globular cluster richness.
AI.result: Galaxies show intermediate-to-old ages (~7 Gyr), low metallicities (~-0.9 dex), and enhanced [Mg/Fe] (~0.3 dex). Six galaxies follow the present-day MZR while the Coma UDG matches a high-z MZR. Radial gradients show two flat-age/mildly-negative-metallicity systems like classical dwarfs and one with a rising metallicity profile. A continuous correlation exists between metallicity gradient and GC richness.
AI.conclusion: Preferential tidal disruption of GCs in the inner regions of GC-rich galaxies can naturally produce rising metallicity profiles, distinguishing them from GC-poor classical dwarfs. This mechanism, possibly coupled with strong early feedback, may explain the unusual metallicity gradients in GC-rich UDGs/NUDGEs.

title: Sudden emergence of a low-frequency hard X-ray lag in the Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 1044
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, accepted by ApJ. Comments are very welcome!
summary: Hard X-ray lags, where low frequency variations in the hard X-ray band lag behind those in the soft band, have been detected in many active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and are generally attributed to the inward propagation of accretion-flow fluctuations through an extended corona. In a long XMM-Newton observation of the Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 1044, we found a remarkable transition in the lag behavior within a single exposure, while the X-ray flux and spectral shape remained largely unchanged. During the first 60 ks, no significant hard X-ray lag was detected, whereas in the subsequent 60 ks, a pronounced lag emerged. The lag was so prominent that a large-amplitude flux variation event during the lag-detected interval, characterized by a gradual dimming followed by recovery, produced a remarkable clockwise loop in the flux-softness diagram. The sudden appearance of the hard X-ray lag suggests that the X-ray corona underwent a rapid transition from a compact to an extended configuration. This scenario is further supported by two independent observational signatures: (1) the variability became noticeably smoother, with a redder power spectral density (PSD), during the lag-detected interval, and (2) the broad Fe K$α$ line profile became narrower and the reflection continuum weaker. These findings highlight the diagnostic power of tracking rapid changes in hard X-ray lags for probing the physical structure and evolution of AGN coronae, and demonstrate that identifying prominent loops in the flux-softness diagram provides an effective way to locate intervals with significant hard X-ray lags.

AI.tldr: In a long XMM-Newton observation of the Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 1044, a sudden transition from no hard X-ray lag to a pronounced hard X-ray lag occurred within a single exposure, despite stable flux and spectral shape. The lag emergence is attributed to a rapid corona transition from compact to extended configuration, supported by redder PSD, a narrower Fe Kα line, and reduced reflection continuum. A clockwise loop in the flux-softness diagram marked the lag-detected interval.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that rapid changes in hard X-ray lags can reveal the physical structure and evolution of AGN coronae, and to establish the flux-softness diagram loop as a diagnostic tool for identifying intervals with significant hard X-ray lags.
AI.method: Analysis of a long XMM-Newton observation of Mrk 1044, examining time-resolved hard X-ray lags, power spectral density, Fe Kα line profile, reflection continuum, and flux-softness diagram behavior within the single exposure.
AI.result: No hard X-ray lag was detected during the first 60 ks, but a pronounced lag emerged in the subsequent 60 ks despite unchanged flux and spectral shape. The lag interval featured a large-amplitude flux variation producing a clockwise loop in the flux-softness diagram, smoother (redder) PSD, narrower Fe Kα line, and weaker reflection continuum.
AI.conclusion: The sudden appearance of the hard X-ray lag indicates a rapid corona transition from a compact to extended configuration. Tracking rapid changes in hard X-ray lags and identifying flux-softness diagram loops are powerful diagnostics for probing AGN corona structure and evolution.

title: Candidates for the most [$O_{III}$] $\lambda5007$-luminous planetary nebula in the Milky Way. I. Integrated light properties of NGC 6572, NGC 6884, and M 1-71
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, accepted in A&A
summary: The bright-end cutoff of the planetary nebula luminosity function (PNLF) serves as an extragalactic standard candle. However, the physical properties of planetary nebulae (PNe) at the PNLF cutoff have been studied only in nearby galaxies, where the PNe appear mostly as point sources. Galactic PNLF is further poorly constrained, primarily due to uncertainties in Galactic PN distances. Following a recent Galactic PNLF survey based on Gaia distances, we aim to characterise PN candidates at the Galactic PNLF cutoff. We observed three PN candidates at the Galactic PNLF cutoff using the Potsdam Multi-Aperture Spectrophotometer (PMAS). We determined their chemical abundances and constructed photoionisation models to derive the central star luminosity (L) and effective temperature (Teff). We constrained the central star masses and most likely distances consistent with the prediction of stellar evolution models. Using these distances, we determined the absolute magnitude M5007. PNe of our sample are located within the top 1 mag of the Galactic PNLF (-4.20 < M5007 <-3.60), with similar nebular properties and a narrow progenitor mass range (1.30-1.75 Msolar). The measured extinction is mostly dominated by the foreground Galactic extinction. The trend between the circum-nebular extinction and central star mass of our PNe is in agreement with those derived in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and M31. All PNe in our sample exhibit weak-emission line star (wels) features in their spectra, but we confirmed that some of these lines originate from the nebula. The PNe are similar in terms of their nebular properties and evolutionary stage. Their characteristics are also consistent with the most [OIII]5007-luminous PNe in the LMC and M31. We demonstrate the importance of circum-nebular extinction and the initial-final mass relation (IFMR) to understand the universality of PNLF as a standard candle.

AI.tldr: The paper studies three planetary nebulae at the bright-end cutoff of the Galactic PNLF using PMAS spectrophotometry and photoionisation modeling. title: Density-induced dark-baryon conversion in $Δ-$admixed hypernuclear neutron stars
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: We investigate density-induced conversion of neutrons into a neutral dark baryon $χ$ in cold, charge-neutral, $β$-equilibrated neutron-star matter containing hyperons and all $Δ(1232)$ quartet. The hadronic sector is modeled within a density-dependent covariant density-functional framework using the DDME2 parametrization. A scalar Higgs portal is included as a possible interaction channel between the visible and dark sectors, although its mean-field contribution is negligible for the couplings adopted here. We find that hyperons and $Δ$ resonances alter the neutron chemical potential, delay the onset of $χ$, and suppress its abundance relative to nucleonic matter. This competition induces characteristic changes in the equation of state, particle fractions, sound speed, and adiabatic index. For $m_χ=1250$, $1300$, and $1400$ MeV, the maximum masses of the complete $N+Y+Δ+χ$ configurations are $1.806$, $1.899$, and $2.024,M_\odot$, respectively, indicating that the massive-pulsar constraint disfavors the lighter dark-baryon benchmarks. The radial profiles further show that for $m_χ=1400$ MeV, $χ$ is confined to the inner core of the most massive stars, while canonical configurations remain essentially unaffected.
